newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Mobile growth seen keeping Nordic telecoms sparky.
newsitem.headline: Mobile growth seen keeping Nordic telecoms sparky.

text.p: Nordic mobile phone firms were propelled further into record territory on Wednesday by better-than-expected Q2 profit from U.S. giant Motorola but analysts remain bullish, especially on Nokia.

The Finnish mobile major, second in the world market after Motorola and number-one in digital, booked the sharpest gains, up over four percent to hit 431 markka at one stage. It only recently conquered the 400-markka barrier in Helsinki.
Ericsson rose a more stately two percent, but was also probing year-high ground at a 327-crown session peak.
"I thought 20 percent upside in six months was not too bad," said Salomon Brothers analyst Douglas Smith of 470-markka 1998 targets for Nokia he set in early June. "I may be forced to change them."

Nokia has been boosted by widening international analyst coverage and market earnings forecast upgrades: its rise for the year to Tuesday was about 60 percent, against 50 percent for Ericsson and about 36 percent for Motorola.
Several London analysts said they were preparing to initiate coverage of Ericsson, pointing generally to favourable views.
Short-term, the temptation to take profits in both stocks may be triggered if Motorola sounds downbeat about cellular market growth at a conference call on Wednesday, analysts said.
One said Motorola's six percent increase in sales of cellular products -- the area the three otherwise quite diverse rivals have in common -- was actually lower than expected.
"If you assume the market is strong and Motorola is relatively weak, then the principle beneficiaries would be Nokia and Ericsson," said Sean Faughnan at JP Morgan in London.
However, he said much would depend on the tone of the conference-call comments.

"Short-term I'm not so bullish on Ericsson," said Stuart Jeffrey at Daiwa Europe in London, who has a "hold" recommendation on the Swedish company. "Nokia I still think there is some upside potential."

Analysts explained the particularly sharp gains in Nokia by its powerful earnings growth potential -- so far it has demonstrated resilience in handset profit margins despite price erosion -- and revived strong sentiment on wireless.
"I like Nokia for a couple of reasons," said Smith. "It is cheap compared to some of its competitors and it's also very focussed on high-growth areas."
Nokia, which overall has greater exposure to fast-growing mobile markets than Ericsson, is an obvious target for an investor convinced by the mobile growth story.
Nokia has forecast mobile users will reach 200 million by the end of this year from 88 million at end 1996, rising to 400-500 million by 2000.
Both Motorola and Ericsson are more widely spread than Nokia: the U.S. company also offers potential for investors seeking a cyclical upturn in semiconductors, for instance.

Ericsson's exposure to less fast-track public switching markets has in the past been viewed by some as a negative, but one analyst mentioned the positive prospect in the near future of the company cutting its R&D spend as a share of sales.
Nokia has traditionally traded at a price-earnings discount to Ericsson, and some analysts talk of potential to revalue it in the sector -- but not those polled on Wednesday.

Based on consensus forecasts from Edinburgh Financial Publications, Nokia's prospective 1997 and 1998 price-earnings ratios were 25 times and 21 times at Tuesday's close: Ericsson traded at 36 and 29 times earnings.
On Jeffrey's forecasts, Nokia's 1997 p/e was 27 -- he saw scope for it to manage 29-30 if overall markets allow. At about 30 he said he would look to take profits.

One analyst said the stock looks more fairly valued on other ratios, citing a fair value to EBITDA earnings before interest, depreciation, taxes and appropriations ratio for Ericsson around 11.5, and for Nokia at 10.5, at Tuesday's close.

Smith said another fundamental supporting Nokia is its relatively high return on capital: "If you are a believer that long-term stock performance is related to return on capital, it's a very positive indication for Nokia."
